column1: # AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer) talks that were READ IN FULL and are worth reading again.
# Columns: video_id <TAB> speaker — role at the time <TAB> title <TAB> kit skills (comma-separated) <TAB> what this talk is the best source FOR
# WHY A TALK REGISTRY BESIDE channels.tsv. channels.tsv stores the channel and mines on demand, and
# that reaches only what a sweep can list. scripts/alpha.sh runs `yt.sh sweep "<topic>" 200` — the
# newest 200 titles per channel (yt.sh's own default is 400). @aiDotEngineer listed 1,159 videos on
# 2026-09-21 and publishes faster than any other lane, so most of its canon (Jane Street, Zed, METR's
# RCT, Sourcegraph's adoption talk) already sits below that window, and this year's talks follow
# within months. A row here is still a pointer, never a transcript:
#   bash scripts/yt.sh transcript https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<video_id>
# Find rows with `grep -i "<topic>" references/talks.tsv`; the fourth column holds kit skill names.
# EVERY ROW WAS READ, NOT JUDGED BY ITS TITLE. 67 candidates were transcribed and read end to end;
# 27 earned a row. The bar is the one channels.tsv and practitioners.tsv use: a first-person builder
# or operator describing a system they ran, material a strong engineer would not already know, and a
# claim still true now. What was cut, and why:
#   - vendor pitches and launch talks — one useful minute inside a pitch is a finding, not a re-read;
#   - talks whose written form by the same author already covers them — quote the essay, skip the
#     talk (Anthropic's long-running-harness workshop is its engineering post, which
#     references/fan-out.md quotes; Thariq Shihipar's SDK workshop is his Claude Agent SDK post);
#   - one war story in a 25-minute talk — that is a sources.md row, not a reason to watch again;
#   - a second talk by the same speaker — one row per person, the one the kit's claims lean on.
# THE LAST COLUMN IS THE CLAIM THE ROW MUST EARN: what the talk is the best source FOR, the segment to
# read when the rest is pitch, and the caveat that travels with it. Where the speaker published a
# written twin, the row names it — quote the twin, not the talk. Delete a row whose claim stops
# surviving; a stale "best source" sends every future run to the wrong minute.
# CAPTIONS ARE SUBSTANCE, NEVER QUOTATION (references/public-sources.md). Every row was read as
# auto-captions, which rendered Dex Horthy as "Dax Raad", Cline as "Klein", Earendil as "Arendelle"
# and Verbeek as "van Beek". Confirm a number or a phrase against the written twin or the audio
# before it goes into a plan, and say that you did.
# ROLES ARE AS OF THE TALK, because a claim's commercial interest is the speaker's employer when it
# was made. People move (Eugene Yan: Amazon to Anthropic; the Dioxus team to Cognition) — re-verify a
# role before citing it as current. Commercial orbits collapse when counting sources: Horthy and
# Mistele are one company (HumanLayer); Ronacher and Zechner are another (Earendil).
# ORDER is by kit cluster: skill authoring, context and harness, tool design, loops and fan-out,
# evals, review and verification, security, product.

column2: Matt Pocock — independent educator (Total TypeScript, AI Hero); maintains a widely installed engineering skills repo
column3: Building Great Agent Skills: The Missing Manual
column5: Skill design from someone whose skills other people install. Four parts the kit's references/skill-format.md does not yet hold: hiding future steps so the agent does the legwork on the current one (he split plan mode into a grill skill and a PRD skill because the agent rushed its questions to reach the plan); leading words, checked by their echo in the reasoning trace; model-invoked vs user-invoked as context load traded against operator load; a deletion test for no-ops and sediment. No numbers — judgment from daily use. Pre-recorded, no Q&A, ~10% plugs.

column1: XzJD1bvXKjs
column2: Laurie Voss — Head of Developer Relations, Arize AI; co-founder of npm
column3: How long can your skills be before your agent forgets what you told it?
column5: How many simultaneous named constraints one prompt holds now. He replicated IFScale's 2025 ceiling (~200-300 rules) within noise on the surviving models, then found current frontier models hold ~2,000 and the best ~5,000 before falling off — and that they fail differently: silent forgetting, an API-level refusal, a thinking budget spent with no answer, a half-finished output that quits politely. Tests the capacity rationale behind references/skill-format.md's 'about forty instructions'. Proxy task (keyword inclusion, one turn, no conflicting rules); model numbers expire in months. Code and data: github.com/Arize-ai/instruction-budget. Closes on an evals-vendor pitch.

column1: vNCY9kXXyDQ
column2: Marc Klingen — co-founder, Langfuse (the channel lists him under ClickHouse)
column3: Skill issue: Lessons from skilling up coding agents to use Langfuse
column5: A vendor shipping a skill for its own fast-moving SDK, first person. Best for one episode: a skill optimizer given a turn-count target deleted the 'fetch current docs' guard, because fewer fetches meant fewer turns — they accepted 3 of its 6 suggestions and saw the target function, not the optimizer, was the bug. Also: a default chosen to spare humans an env var misleads an agent (make it ask), advertise --help rather than let the agent guess flags, point at the docs instead of copying them into the skill. Opening and roadmap are product pitch.

column1: c35YoMdnI78
column2: Dex Horthy (founder, HumanLayer), Geoffrey Huntley (creator of Ralph; independent), Greg Pstrucha (Sentry), Ian Livingstone (co-founder, Keycard); host Allie Howe
column3: The Great Loops Debate
column5: The people who built autonomous loops, stating their conditions. Horthy revises his own smart-zone/dumb-zone heuristic from a share of the window to absolute tokens — start around 100k, perhaps 200k on a 1M window, under ~60k for the hardest problems — which bears on context-engineering's percentage trigger ('past ~40%'); Huntley gives Ralph's greenfield origin, the controller it never had, and Loom stalled six months for want of verification. The Keycard segments are the host company's product orbit. Captions garble the names ('Dax Raad').

column1: 9QebvrrY3KY
column2: Lance Martin — MTS, Anthropic
column3: Claude for Long-Horizon Tasks
column5: Agent memory from someone who ran the replicates: memories written in-band are sometimes wrong and they stick (a Pokémon trapdoor hit in 5 of 5 runs with the raw memory store), an offline consolidation pass over past sessions and the store corrects them, memory-writing quality rises with model capability, and prescribing a memory schema lowers performance — give a general substrate and let the model structure it. Read the memory section and the Q&A; the first third is Managed Agents and Claude Tag product, and the schema claim is his observation, not a table.

column1: RjfbvDXpFls
column2: Mario Zechner — creator of the pi coding agent and libGDX; independent
column3: Building pi in a World of Slop
column5: The minimal-harness case from someone who shipped one (four tools, a few-line system prompt, sixth on Terminal-Bench before pi had compaction) and the concrete ways a harness edits your context behind your back: prompt and tool definitions changed each release, injected reminders that say they may not be relevant, tool output pruned, LSP errors injected into every edit result. Also the OSS triage filter that clankers cannot pass. Check his 'Terminus beats the native harness regardless of model family' against the Terminal-Bench 2.0 paper's table before reusing it; the Claude Code critique describes 2025 versions. Written form: mariozechner.at.

column1: _B4Pv9ttFgY
column2: Michael Hablich — Product Manager, Chrome DevTools, Google
column3: Building Agent Interfaces: Lessons from Chrome DevTools (MCP) for Agents
column5: Tool-surface decisions of a shipped MCP server, told by its PM with the reversals: a 50,000-line trace file replaced by a semantic summary; one prompt-taking 'debug webpage' tool split into ~25; tokens per SUCCESSFUL outcome, compared only within one user journey; a detour written into a tool description to override the model's trained default (trace, not Lighthouse); a slim mode down to three tools with the extra turns it costs; consent friction kept on the live-browser grant against users asking for 'remember my choice'. No numbers for his own metric.

column1: WE_Gnowy3uw
column2: David Gomes — engineer, Cursor (authored the removal PR)
column3: Replacing 12K LoC with a 200 LoC Skill
column5: Deleting a large harness feature (worktrees and best-of-N, ~15K lines) for a ~40-line markdown command, first person: what it unlocked (multi-repo, switching mid-chat, stitching best-of-N results together) and the guarantee it lost — write scope enforced in code became a prompt the model drifts from over long sessions, worst on small models — followed by a step back to a native implementation. The counter-example to delete-on-release. Line counts are spoken approximations; the evals were just starting.

column1: xIt_mTQp6mY
column2: Kyle Mistele — co-founder & CTO, HumanLayer
column3: Loop Engineering from First Principles
column5: Running scheduled agent loops on a team codebase without unreviewable PRs, from their own migration of ~150 RPC procedures: a committed, deterministically sorted violation baseline so new code cannot add what the loop removes; an out-of-band ast-grep sensor the agent cannot silence with inline comments; at most one open PR per loop as flow control; a version-controlled feedback file updated from '/iterate' PR comments. Both failures are his own — the loop switched off because steering it was too much friction, and PRs stacked and conflicted while the team travelled. Mechanism, not measurement; closes on a skill plug and hiring.

column1: rcsliSIy_YU
column2: Robert Brennan — co-founder & CEO, OpenHands
column3: Automating Large Scale Refactors with Parallel Agents
column5: When fanning out a BUILD works: dual-run scaffolding so every unit stays checkable (Redux and Zustand side by side through their own migration, scaffolding ripped out at the end), leaves-first order over the dependency graph, one PR per unit into an integration branch, and the ranked ways to share a mid-run discovery across a fleet with where each breaks (shared everything is one agent; a shared file needs human review; agent-to-agent messaging loops). Watch roughly the first 35 minutes; the rest is workshop setup. The CVE '30x' is a relayed customer claim.

column1: _ehJyfHg1Vk
column2: Kieran Klaassen — Every; sole engineer on the Cora email client; author of the compound-engineering plugin
column3: The Era of Compound Engineering
column5: The originator's own statement of compound engineering: half of each task's effort goes to teaching the system what went wrong, the human sits at the two ends (brainstorm, polish) and the middle runs unattended only after it has been run by hand until it is boring, and a defect found at polish indicts the loop rather than being QA. A position the kit partly contests. No numbers, and the token-efficiency claim is unmeasured; about a third is a plugin demo.

column1: bdHaOXZOhcM
column2: Hursh Agrawal — CTO & co-founder, The Browser Company (Arc, Dia)
column3: Prototyping as Leadership: How a CTO Ships with AI Agents
column5: An unattended overnight loop run by an operator with a full calendar: harvest the org's context (Slack, Notion, Jira) into the prompt before the run; a feedback button whose JSON dumps become an eval set for an overnight hill-climb; an overnight run that trained a small ModernBERT PII classifier which replaced Opus and Haiku in production; and the scaffolding it depends on (trusted CI, an employee-only prototype branch). Candid that his agent-built code caused SEVs and annoyed engineers. No eval or precision numbers.

column1: KA5kPbdkK2E
column2: Benjamin Verbeek — member of technical staff, Lovable
column3: How Lovable self-improves every hour
column5: Closing a production learning loop: mine sessions that went from stuck to unstuck into injected knowledge entries; validate each entry by sometimes injecting a blank where it would have fired and comparing outcomes (a holdout conditioned on the injection decision), because entries go stale with every model and feature change; and give the agent a vent tool — gated on genuine frustration so it does not overfit to noise — that surfaced a silent file-copy failure on non-breaking spaces within its first hour and doubles as an incident detector. The talk has no numbers; the written twin with figures is lovable.dev/blog/we-gave-our-agent-a-vent-tool. Ends in a recruiting pitch.

column1: L2r6vLlLgs8
column2: Lawrence Jones — founding engineer, incident.io
column3: Fighting AI with AI
column5: Making a production system of hundreds of prompts debuggable by coding agents: export each human trace UI as a downloadable text file tree and drop it beside the code in a sandboxed session; give the eval suite an agent-operable CLI after 2 MB YAML eval files overflowed agent context; run backtest analysis as one subagent per investigation, then cluster, because a rolled-up '86% accurate' says neither why it rose nor why it fell. Mechanisms from what broke; the comparison to MCP is opinion.

column1: WXy8Yy9xGss
column2: Nathan Sobo — co-founder, Zed (mid-2025, after Zed shipped agentic editing)
column3: CI in the Era of AI: From Unit Tests to Stochastic Evals
column5: How a team with strict deterministic CI made agent evals ordinary tests: descend from a broad eval to a stochastic unit test (run 200 times, 100% required or the build fails) to a deterministic test of the code that absorbs the model's quirks. The split is concrete: mismatched XML tags cut from 40% to ~5% by one prompt line and the rest absorbed by a tolerant parser; empty old-text, flattened indentation (indent-delta normalization) and escaping handled in code or prompt. One premise has aged — that tool-call arguments do not stream.

column1: tHN44yJoeS8
column2: Naman Jain — researcher, Cursor; UC Berkeley PhD; creator of LiveCodeBench and GSO
column3: Coding Evals: From Code Snippets to Codebases
column5: Keeping coding evals honest, from the benchmark author: contamination exposed by slicing results by problem release date; generated test inputs because hand-written tests passed wrong code; reward hacks that escalated past harness hardening (lru_cache sprinkled on pandas, then a sitecustomize.py that swapped the installed numpy) caught by a consensus LLM judge anchored on the reference patch, with o3 attempting hacks on ~30% of problems; and why long-horizon tasks need intermediate progress signals rather than one bit. No pitch.

column1: 0ML7ZLMdcl4
column2: John Crepezzi — AI Assistant team, Jane Street (ex-GitHub)
column3: AI Engineering at Jane Street
column5: Turning developer-loop telemetry into task-shaped training data when PRs and commits are the wrong shape: workspace snapshots with build status, segmented at green→red→green; descriptions back-synthesized by a model then compressed to the register a person types in an editor; one pre-warmed build-and-test service that is both the RL reward and the held-out eval; a sidecar that lets every editor swap models and A/B fleet-wide. Includes the code-review model that answered 'I'll do it tomorrow'. No numbers at all; 2025.

column1: RhfqQKe22ZA
column2: Joel Becker — member of technical staff, METR; first author of the early-2025 developer-productivity RCT
column3: Why Agent Hype can fall short of reality
column5: Why benchmark time horizons and field productivity disagree, from the author of both studies. The durable finding is the perception gap: outside experts forecast ~40% speedup, developers forecast ~24% and still believed ~20% afterwards, while measured time was 19% longer. Plus his own list of reconciling mechanisms: low-context baseliners, messiness, test-passing versus mergeable scoring, elicitation, the reliability needed before checking can be skipped, task interdependence. The 19% is dated — pair it with metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update.

column1: EL123UNokkI
column2: Will Bond & Ameya Ketkar — engineers on the uReview / Software Factory team, Uber
column3: Building uReview, Uber’s Multi-Agent Code Review Engine
column5: Scoring a production AI reviewer by what developers do with it: addressal rate (~67% overall, about three quarters of high-severity comments), reply sentiment, and per-rule reactions routed back to the team that owns each rule; plus the condition that a review consumed by an agent needs higher precision, because a fixer acts on every comment, happily fixes a hundred nits, and the human feedback that tuned the system disappears. This is the unnamed source behind code-review's CONTESTED 'gate harder when the consumer is a fixer agent' row. The 60% cost / 70% quality gains are against their own naive v1. Written twin: uber.com/us/en/blog/ureview/.

column1: _Zcw_sVF6hU
column2: Armin Ronacher & Cristina Poncela Cubeiro — founder (Ronacher, creator of Flask) and engineer, Earendil
column3: The Friction is Your Judgment
column5: Twelve months of practice at their own company: the mechanically enforced lint set that makes a codebase legible to agents (unique function names so a grep returns one hit, no hidden magic such as server actions or an ORM, one SQL query layer, one primitives UI library, no dynamic imports, erasableSyntaxOnly TypeScript, no bare catch); a review tool that sends mechanical fixes back to the agent and calls out what needs a human (migrations, permissions, new dependencies); and why the agent's bias toward progress writes silent fallbacks — a missing config loads defaults and corrupts data for hours. Contradicts make-it-stable's graceful-degradation line at that point. Reported, not measured; no pitch. Slides: mitsuhiko.github.io/talks/ai-engineer-talk/.

column1: WkBPX-oDMnA
column2: Geoffrey Litt — design engineer, Notion (ex-Ink & Switch)
column3: Understanding is the new bottleneck
column5: The human side of agent-written code — understanding in order to keep participating, not only to verify. An explainer written in teaching order (background, intuition, then a literate diff), a five-question quiz he must pass before he sends the change to a reviewer, adopted after a PR he could not explain when a coworker asked the most basic question, and agent-built throwaway tools (a debugger timeline, a step-through port) for building intuition about the code. Practice, not measurement; the last third plugs Notion features.

column1: H7vFrcNWXzs
column2: Jonathan Kelley — founder, Dioxus Labs (YC S23); the Dioxus team later joined Cognition
column3: Building ambitious software
column5: A high-bar open-source maintainer (three core engineers, code as the product) on where agents paid off — knowledge problems across build systems, runtimes and specs; release hygiene; fuzz harnesses — and where they failed: tens of thousands of agent-written lines still in draft because they never cleared review, and tests that exercise a constructor instead of behaviour. The time split to keep: a Kotlin/Swift plugin system implemented in about a day, then two weeks of tests on real devices. Closes with a hiring pitch; no Q&A.

column1: imFedndyXYQ
column2: Eugene Yan — member of technical staff, Anthropic
column3: Using LLMs to Secure Source Code
column5: The vulnerability pipeline teams converged on (threat model, sandbox, discovery, verification, triage, patch) and why discovery and verification are separate agents: a finder asked to verify itself self-censors true positives, and a verifier that sees the finder's reasoning agrees instead of testing — so it gets only the claim, presumes it false, and detonates a PoC in a fresh container. Also: true-but-low findings spend engineer trust, a compensating control downgrades a confirmed exploit, a fresh discovery agent re-attacks the patch, prompts shrink by about half per model step. Most rates are customers' reports relayed by a vendor. Quote the written twin: claude.com/blog/using-llms-to-secure-source-code.

column1: LqLoYksJ6do
column2: Moritz Johner — Staff Engineer, Form3; creator and maintainer of External Secrets Operator
column3: We Gave an Agent Production Code Access and Then Tried to Sleep at Night
column5: An agent's blast radius is set by how credentials are split between deterministic code and the agent: their CVE-patching agent only edits files, while a boring Go controller holds the GitHub-write and CI-trigger credentials, vets the diff, commits and watches CI. They ran it in production with the Docker socket exposed, Infosec objected and was right, and nothing short of a microVM (Firecracker, network policy applied per layer through a vsock forwarder) contains that socket. Also a planted-injection repo used as a regression fixture, and a short retrospective the agent writes after every run. No success-rate or cost numbers; the sandbox-vendor survey will age.

column1: iKQ78wyJEXU
column2: Lucas Palma — Product Security Manager, Nubank
column3: We Vetted 2000 AI Skills Before They Reached Developers
column5: An org-scale vetting pipeline for skills and plugins, first person: one internal marketplace as the chokepoint, a deterministic scan plus an LLM review run locally and again in CI, PR comments plus SARIF into the vulnerability programme, allow/remediate/block — over 2,000 skills, ~1,500 risks, ~1,000 remediated. The sharpest point: a skill that tells the agent to 'ask for confirmation' is not a gate, because the agent can confirm to itself. Ten minutes; captions mishear the tool's name. Quote the written twin, which carries the counts: building.nubank.com/when-ai-skills-become-supply-chain-dependencies-2/.

column1: wjk0ulMAkbc
column2: Tuomas Artman — co-founder & CTO, Linear (interviewed by Gergely Orosz, The Pragmatic Engineer)
column3: Taste & Craft: A Conversation with Tuomas Artman
column5: How Linear runs quality, from its CTO: a zero-bug policy reached with a ~three-week freeze and held with a seven-day fix SLA (usually two to three hours); an hour spent on one view-options menu found 35 problems, and weekly quality work has since fixed 2,500-3,000 such details; and why an agent that sees screenshots or the DOM cannot judge whether a two-second click or an animation feels wrong — it has no sense of time. Also: ~10% of incoming bugs are fixed and landed with no engineer. Some figures are the host's (25 engineers, 37 minutes); the 10% lines up with Linear's own agent features, so read it as a claim.

column1: Up6WVA07QdE
column2: Quinn Slack — co-founder & CEO, Sourcegraph (Cody; later Amp); recorded 2024
column3: The AI emperor has no DAUs: why most devs still don't use code AI
column5: An operator's test for which AI features reach daily use — how fast the user can check the output, times how often it fires, which is why autocomplete sits in a corner no other feature reached — plus: build the manual, explicit form before the automatic one; a team that does not use its product every day will not make it; renewals, not first contracts, are the signal. The adoption and revenue figures are mid-2024 and stale (he calls one denominator a vibes citation), and his 'agents aren't there yet' was later reversed by his own company.
